name: Cold showers

lead: Cold showers are taken for claimed benefits to skin, hair, testosterone, mood and discipline. Users post that skin and hair look better; others say cold showers make eye bags or features look harsher.

Cold exposure triggers the cold shock response, vasoconstriction and a surge in the sympathetic nervous system, and repeated cold showers reduce the initial response to later cold immersion. Meta-analyses of cold-water exposure report pooled signals toward better mood, perceived stress and wellbeing, with wide confidence intervals. No study has tested cold showers for skin appearance or testosterone.

paras: People end a normal shower with a cold blast or take the whole shower cold, often as a morning routine, building up duration over days to weeks. It overlaps with ice baths, cold plunges and the Wim Hof Method.

Cold-water immersion can cause gasping, heart rate and blood pressure surges, and arrhythmias in some people. The American Heart Association and British Heart Foundation advise consulting a physician before cold therapy. Combining breath-holding or hyperventilation with water has been linked to blackout and drowning reports.

angle.text: Users take cold showers expecting tighter-looking, healthier skin, better hair and a mood and discipline lift, through a circulation and stress-response jolt. Meta-analyses report mood and stress effects; skin, hair and hormone claims come from user reports.

lead: Cold showers are showers taken with cold water, used in looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities for claimed effects on skin, hair, testosterone, mood and discipline.[1][2] The practice overlaps with ice baths, cold plunges and the Wim Hof Method.[3]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials of cold-water immersion in healthy adults assessed outcomes including sleep, stress, fatigue, skin health, immunity, mood and anxiety, and a 2026 meta-analysis of 13 studies found pooled estimates generally favoured cold-water exposure for depressive symptoms, perceived stress, wellbeing and mood, but with wide confidence intervals and attenuated results in controlled-only analyses.[4][5] No study was found testing cold showers for testosterone or facial appearance.

paras: Cold showers use water below comfortable temperature, from brief cold finishes to full cold showers. Studies of cold-water immersion define the exposure as water at or below 15 degrees Celsius for at least 30 seconds, delivered through showers, ice baths or plunges.[4]

A 1964 Journal of Applied Physiology paper studied cardiovascular responses to ice-cold showers, and a 1970 study examined how length of cold showers affects skin temperature and exercise heart rate.[6][7]

Posters claim cold showers improve skin and hair, reduce hair loss, support testosterone and discipline, and act as a 'cope destroyer' that builds mental toughness.[8][9][10] Some say they help with premature ejaculation, sperm count and gynecomastia, claims made in a thread that other members treated as humorous.[2]

Critics on the same forum say cold showers can make facial features look harsher, thicken beard and body hair, or worsen under-eye bags by affecting circulation, and some assert that cold-shower habits are overrated.[11]

The 2025 PLOS ONE meta-analysis included 11 randomized studies with 3,177 participants, almost all using baths rather than showers, and listed skin health among the outcomes it evaluated.[4] The 2026 Frontiers in Physiology meta-analysis of 13 studies with 4,105 participants found pooled estimates favoured cold exposure for depression symptoms, perceived stress, wellbeing and mood, little consistent benefit for anxiety, and sparse data on sleep, cortisol, heart rate and pain.[5]

A 2008 hypothesis paper proposed adapted cold showers as a potential treatment for depression, and a 2005 study found repeated cold showers reduced the initial responses to later cold-water immersion.[12][13] Two randomized trials of the Wim Hof Method, which combines fast-paced breathing with cold showers, in women with high stress and depressive symptoms compared it with slow-breathing controls; in one trial all four arms improved with no group differences at the end of the intervention.[14][15]

Wikipedia reports that a 2024 meta-analysis of the Wim Hof Method judged most studies to be of very low quality, and that the American Heart Association and British Heart Foundation advise consulting a physician before cold therapy.[3]

Wikipedia reports that cold-water immersion can trigger heart arrhythmias in healthy people, and that the Wim Hof breathing exercises can cause hyperventilation and potentially fatal blackout if done in water, with 32 alleged deaths linked to the method as of March 2024.[3]

No studies found of cold showers for skin appearance, hair or testosterone. Human research examines mood, stress and wellbeing outcomes of cold-water exposure, habituation to cold, and the Wim Hof Method for depressive symptoms.[4][5][13][14]

lore.intro: Cold showers are a recurring topic on looksmax.org, discussed as a skin and hair aid, a discipline tool, a source of jokes, and, by some, a downside for appearance.[2][8][11]
